period_summary: Citations are densest in the 2nd–4th centuries CE, particularly in apologetic and christological contexts. This concentration reflects the verse's central role in early Christian debates about the divine sonship of Jesus, driving intensive engagement with its exact wording.

citations.cited_text: Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Justin's wording matches the LXX verbatim: 'Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε.' No deviation from the standard Septuagintal text is evident, including the Greek perfect γεγέννηκά rather than any rendering closer to the Hebrew qatal form.
citations.theological_use: Justin uses the verse to argue that Jesus is the pre-existent divine Son declared at his baptism and at the resurrection, defending Christian christology against Jewish interlocutors who restricted the verse to Solomon or Hezekiah.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's citation confirms that by the mid-2nd century a stable Greek LXX text of Ps 2:7 was in wide circulation in Asia Minor and Rome and was used as the authoritative scriptural base for christological argument.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus's Old Latin citation 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te' is a direct Latin rendering of the LXX Vorlage and corresponds to what would become the standard Vetus Latina text; it does not reflect any distinctively Hebraizing variant.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus deploys the verse to demonstrate the eternal generation of the Son and to ground the incarnation in scriptural prophecy, countering Gnostic denigrations of the material birth of Christ.
citations.transmission_implication: Irenaeus's Vetus Latina form shows that the LXX-based text had already been rendered into Latin by the late 2nd century and was liturgically and theologically established in the Western church.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Latin wording aligns with the Vetus Latina / LXX tradition; there is no sign of the MT's slightly different nuance nor of any unique Carthaginian variant.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian cites the verse in his anti-Monarchian polemic to establish the distinct personal identity of the Son ('tu') from the Father ('ego'), making the pronouns themselves carry theological weight.
citations.transmission_implication: The agreement of Tertullian with Irenaeus in a shared Vetus Latina form indicates a stable, geographically widespread Latin translation tradition anchored to the Greek LXX, not to the Hebrew.

citations.chapter_section: De Princ. I.2.4; Comm. Jo. I.32
citations.cited_text: Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Origen cites the standard LXX text but in his Hexaplaric discussions also engages with the Hebrew and notes variants from Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion; his awareness of the Hebrew tradition means his commentary reflects both the LXX form and Hebraizing alternatives, producing a mixed textual consciousness even when he formally cites the LXX.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses Ps 2:7 in the context of the eternal generation of the Son, interpreting 'today' (σήμερον) as denoting atemporal divine eternity rather than a historical moment, anticipating Nicene theology.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexaplaric awareness is crucial: his citations show that multiple Greek versions (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) of Ps 2:7 were in circulation by the 3rd century, complicating the picture of a single stable LXX text.

citations.cited_text: Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius cites the verse in its standard LXX form and in his Psalms commentary explicitly engages the Hexaplaric column differences; where he quotes the running text he uses the LXX, demonstrating the dominance of the Septuagintal form in 4th-century Caesarean scholarship.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius applies Ps 2:7 both to the eternal divine begetting and to the historical resurrection, noting Acts 13:33 as the apostolic hermeneutical key, thereby tying the verse to a christological-exegetical tradition stretching back to Paul.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius's Caesarean citations, enriched by the Hexapla, confirm that by the early 4th century the LXX form was treated as canonical while Hebrew variants were known but marginalized in Christian usage.

citations.cited_text: Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius cites the LXX form without deviation and explicitly rejects any interpretation that would make 'today' refer to a temporal beginning of the Son's existence, insisting on the eternal sense; his text agrees perfectly with the Göttingen LXX reconstructed text of Psalm 2:7.
citations.theological_use: Athanasius deploys the verse as a cornerstone of anti-Arian christology: 'today' denotes the eternal Now of the Father's begetting, not a moment in time, thus supporting the homoousios position.
citations.transmission_implication: Athanasius's precise LXX citation in a polemical context shows that the Septuagintal text had become the normative scriptural authority in Alexandrian theological discourse with no perceived need to consult the Hebrew.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Hilary's Latin follows the Vetus Latina / Old Latin tradition consistently and does not show the influence of Jerome's later Hebraizing revisions; his form 'ego hodie genui te' reflects the LXX's perfect tense translated into Latin as a perfect, not a present.
citations.theological_use: Hilary employs the verse to defend the eternal generation of the Son against Arian subordinationism, insisting that 'I have begotten' refers to a non-temporal divine act and not to the nativity or resurrection alone.
citations.transmission_implication: Hilary's pre-Hieronymian Latin citation confirms that the Old Latin tradition, derived from the LXX, was still the Western standard before Jerome's Gallican and Hebrew Psalters began to displace it.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Augustine cites primarily the Old Latin / Vetus Latina form but shows awareness of Jerome's newer translations; he occasionally notes that 'today' (hodie) might be understood temporally (as in the resurrection reading of Acts 13:33) or eternally, suggesting sensitivity to the range of interpretations without adopting a divergent text form.
citations.theological_use: Augustine uses the verse both in its eternal-generation sense and in its resurrection-application sense (following Acts 13:33), demonstrating a sophisticated two-level christological hermeneutic that became influential in Western exegesis.
citations.transmission_implication: Augustine's mixed textual engagement, aware of both the Vetus Latina and Jerome's revisions, marks a transitional moment in Western transmission where the LXX-derived Old Latin was beginning to face competition from proto-Vulgate traditions.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history of Psalm 2:7 reveals an overwhelmingly uniform reliance on the LXX text form across both Greek and Latin traditions from the 2nd through the 5th centuries, with no Church Father up to Augustine showing direct dependence on the Hebrew MT for the running citation. The LXX text 'Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε' and its Vetus Latina derivative 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te' functioned as the uncontested scriptural base for christological argument in both East and West. The only disruption to this uniformity comes from Origen's Hexaplaric awareness and Augustine's late transitional awareness of Hieronymian alternatives, neither of which displaced the LXX form in practice. This pattern strongly implies that the LXX rendering of Ps 2:7 was fixed and authoritative in Christian communities well before the patristic period proper, and that the Hebrew tradition was encountered as a scholarly curiosity rather than a competing canonical authority.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Almost every major early Christian writer who quoted Psalm 2:7 used the same Greek (or Latin translated from Greek) version of the text, not the Hebrew. This consistency across different regions and centuries shows that the Greek translation of the Old Testament was the Bible of the early church, and Psalm 2:7 was particularly important because it seemed to speak directly about Jesus as God's Son.

notable_variants.reading: 'ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε' (I today have begotten you) — LXX perfect tense
notable_variants.significance: The Greek perfect γεγέννηκά (I have begotten) allows the eternal-generation interpretation that became central to Nicene theology, whereas the Hebrew qatal could be rendered as a simple past; the LXX's Greek perfect thus carried enormous theological freight in patristic christological disputes.

notable_variants.reading: 'ego hodie genui te' (I today begot you) — Vetus Latina / Old Latin form
notable_variants.significance: The Old Latin 'genui' (I begot/have begotten) directly mirrors the LXX perfect, confirming that the Latin translation tradition was made from the Greek and not from the Hebrew, and that no independent Hebraizing Latin tradition existed for this verse before Jerome.

notable_variants.reading: Application to the Resurrection (Acts 13:33 interpretive link)
notable_variants.significance: Some fathers, following the NT use of Ps 2:7 in Acts 13:33, read the verse as fulfilled in the resurrection rather than the eternal generation; while not a textual variant per se, this hermeneutical divergence reflects how the LXX text form was stable enough to support multiple theological readings simultaneously.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX Perfect Tense Drove Nicene Christological Orthodoxy
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The single most significant implication of this patristic citation history is that the theological distinctiveness of the Greek LXX's perfect tense γεγέννηκά — absent as such from the Hebrew MT — became the linguistic foundation on which the doctrine of eternal generation was constructed. Without access to or interest in the MT form, patristic theologians worked exclusively from a text that grammatically implied an atemporal, completed divine act, which the Nicene tradition then systematized. This means that a translation choice embedded in the LXX had direct and traceable consequences for the dogmatic development of Trinitarian theology.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The Greek translation of Psalm 2:7 used a verb form (the perfect tense) that made it sound like an eternal, timeless act rather than a historical event, and early Christian writers built their understanding of Jesus as the eternal Son of God largely on that specific wording. If they had read the Hebrew original more closely, the theological argument might have taken a different shape.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis correctly identifies the dominant LXX/Vetus Latina pattern for Ps 2:7 in patristic citation, but several specific chapter/section references and attributions require verification and one citation appears misattributed.

flagged_claims.claim: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho ch. 88, 'Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε'
flagged_claims.reason: Justin cites Ps 2:7 in Dialogue with Trypho 88, but he is well known for citing this verse with the variant 'Son art thou; this day have I begotten thee' in connection with the baptism of Jesus, and notably elsewhere (Dial. 103) links it to a textual form that may reflect Luke 3:22 D. The bare claim that Justin's wording 'matches the LXX verbatim' with 'no deviation' overlooks Justin's known textual peculiarities at this verse.

flagged_claims.claim: Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses III.18.3, 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te'
flagged_claims.reason: Adv. Haer. III.18.3 discusses the recapitulation but the specific Ps 2:7 citation is more securely located elsewhere (e.g., Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching 49); the chapter reference should be verified.

flagged_claims.claim: Tertullian, Adversus Praxean ch. 7, 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te'
flagged_claims.reason: Tertullian cites Ps 2:7 in Adv. Praxean (notably ch. 11 and elsewhere) and in Adv. Marcionem; the specific assignment to ch. 7 needs verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen, De Principiis I.2.4; Commentary on John I.32
flagged_claims.reason: Origen's discussion of eternal generation in De Principiis I.2 does engage Ps 2:7-related themes, but the precise section numbers and the specific Comm. Jo. I.32 citation should be verified; Origen's book/section numbering varies across editions.
Eusebius treats Ps 2 extensively in DE IV and VII; the specific section IV.15 needs verification as the locus for this citation.
Athanasius discusses Ps 2:7 in the Orations against the Arians, but the principal locus is generally identified in Or. IV or earlier sections; II.62 needs verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Hilary of Poitiers, De Trinitate III.11
flagged_claims.reason: Hilary discusses Ps 2:7 across De Trinitate (notably books VI and XII as well); the specific assignment to III.11 should be checked.

flagged_claims.claim: his text agrees perfectly with the Göttingen LXX reconstructed text of Psalm 2:7
flagged_claims.reason: The Göttingen Septuaginta volume for the Psalter has not yet been published (as of recent scholarship); referencing 'the Göttingen LXX reconstructed text' for Psalms is anachronistic/unverifiable. Rahlfs-Hanhart is the standard critical edition.
Augustine was bishop of Hippo Regius, not Carthage; the regional tag is imprecise (though both are in Roman North Africa).

flagged_claims.claim: Origen's citations show that multiple Greek versions (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) of Ps 2:7 were in circulation by the 3rd century
flagged_claims.reason: While Origen's Hexapla included these versions, the specific extant readings of Aquila/Symmachus/Theodotion at Ps 2:7 should be verified before claiming Origen's citations document them; the analysis does not quote any actual variant.

safe_claims: The LXX reads 'Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε'
The Vetus Latina form 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te' is a direct rendering of the LXX
Acts 13:33 applies Ps 2:7 to the resurrection
The Greek perfect γεγέννηκά supported eternal-generation readings in Nicene theology
Jerome later produced Hebraizing Psalter revisions that differed from the Vetus Latina
Ps 2:7 was central to early Christian christological argument
